inline.s: In explaining this sutra now, we first interpret the title, then clarify the history of its translation, and finally expound the sutra text.
The Buddha Speaks the Sutra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life

According to the text below, when Ananda asked, the Buddha established two titles. The first states: This sutra is named for the contemplation of the land of Ultimate Bliss, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, and the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta. Adding the word sutra, it totals twenty characters, named from the mind and its objects. It also says: It is also called Purifying the Karmic Obstructions and Being Born Before the Buddhas. Adding the word sutra, it totals nine characters, named from breaking through obstructions and reaping the reward. In the first title, the single character contemplation is the wisdom that contemplates; the following eighteen characters are the objects contemplated. The land of Ultimate Bliss is the circumstantial reward, which envelops the first six contemplations (1. the Sun, 2. the Water, 3. the Ground, 4. the Trees, 5. the Pools, 6. the Comprehensive). From Immeasurable Life onward is the primary reward, which envelops the last ten (7. the Lotus Seat, 8. the Sacred Images, 9. the Buddha's Body, 10. Avalokiteshvara, 11. Mahasthamaprapta, 12. the Universal Rebirth, 13. the Mixed Thoughts of Buddha and Bodhisattvas, 14. the Highest Grade, 15. the Middle Grade, 16. the Lowest Grade). Contemplating the Buddha in total matches the former three contemplations; the two Bodhisattvas in total embrace the seven contemplations. Thus this one title contains all sixteen. In the second title, Purifying the Karmic Obstructions is the power and function of the sixteen contemplations as a whole; when contemplation is accomplished and obstructions break, that is the immediate cause. Being Born Before the Buddhas is the future fruit. It does not point to Amitabha alone but says the Buddhas, because the sutra below says: Whoever sees the Buddha of Immeasurable Life sees the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions. The present translator uses only the first title, following what is concise, yet, since it accords with the Buddhas, it deeply matches the intent of the sutra. The Tiantai Commentary says: Raising the primary reward to gather in the circumstantial reward, and describing the transforming teacher to include the assembly; though the contemplations are sixteen, naming the Buddha suffices. This is an interpretation that raises the essential to embrace both the preceding and following. Master Huiyuan's Commentary says: This sutra takes contemplating the Buddha as its chief focus, so he is singled out. This is an interpretation holding that the various contemplations follow the essential aim of the sutra. Examining the two explanations, the latter meaning is the most complete. For regarding contemplation of the Buddha as the primary meaning, the land must first be set forth as the gradual entry; afterward, from contemplating the Buddha, one extends to the assembly to reveal its universality. Hence the passage on contemplating the Buddha alone is called the samadhi of recollecting the Buddha.

In the title, the upper seven characters form the specific title, specific to this text; the single lower character is the common title, extending to all scriptures. The upper two denote the Buddha who proclaims the teaching; the lower five show the practice taught.

First, in the proclaimer, Buddha is one of the ten epithets. To speak means to delight and satisfy the minds of the assembly (Note: this is said with reference to the hearers, hence to delight and satisfy the minds of the assembly. The Tiantai Commentary says: To speak is to delight what is held in mind. The Miaozong Sub-commentary explains: Delight is to be fully pleased. Mind is what is held within. As to this sutra, it is that the Tathagata, through long cultivation and realization, holds within him the samadhi of recollecting the Buddha; now that the capacity is stirred, speaking it gives full expression to what was formerly held in mind). The transforming teacher of this world is surely Sakyamuni, so only his common epithet is raised. The objects contemplated below, lest they be confused with other honored ones, have both the common and specific titles raised. According to the Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom: scriptures may be spoken by five kinds of persons — Buddhas, holy disciples, sages, gods and dragons and ghosts, and persons of transformation. To show that this sutra was spoken by the Buddha himself and to exclude other persons, so that faith and acceptance might arise. Yet within one age of the teaching, the discipline is spoken only by the Buddha, specially set forth as most profound and secret; the scriptures may be spoken by others but must receive the Buddha's seal. Still, within the scriptures, the Pure Land teaching is certainly spoken by the Buddha, showing it is beyond the knowledge of lesser sages and ordinary beings. Hence the other sutras may sometimes omit the mark, but all the Pure Land sutras must be so distinguished.

Second, in the teaching spoken, the first character above is the mind that contemplates; the four below are the objects contemplated. In the first part, both the great and lesser contemplation methods point to the sixth consciousness as the substance that contemplates. Among the five aggregates it belongs to the aggregate of volitional formations. The three preceding minds are in substance merely neutral; one must take the volitional mind that forms karma before it can recompense and draw forth rebirth. According to the text below, it is sometimes called recollection and sometimes reflection; the names differ but the substance is the same, and all point to mental intention as that which contemplates. (The above are all recorded from the Lingzhi Commentary.)

The Meaning of Mahayana, chapter two says: Coarse reflection is called applied thought and subtle reflection sustained thought. The Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom, chapter seventeen: Question: Are applied thought and sustained thought one dharma or two? Answer: They are two. The coarse mind of the first moment is applied thought; the subtle analysis is sustained thought. For example, when a bell is struck, the first loud sound is applied thought, the later subtle sound sustained thought. (Annotated Commentary)

Next, in the object contemplated, in Sanskrit it is called Amitabha, translated as Immeasurable Life and also as Immeasurable Light. Life represents merit, the virtue of liberation; light represents wisdom, the virtue of prajna. Prajna and liberation together adorn the dharmakaya, and this is the Buddha who saves beings in the land of shared reward. The successor Avalokiteshvara truly has a measured span of life, but with reference to ordinary and lesser beings who cannot count it, it is called immeasurable. Buddha, fully stated as buddha, is translated as the awakened one. Awakening has two meanings: the meaning of awareness, for the four fetters are like robbers that only the sage perceives so they can do no harm; and the meaning of realization, for ignorance is like sleep, and once the wisdom of the sage arises it is like waking. Confronted with the two vehicles, he is called the Great Awakened One; surpassing the stage of equal awakening, he is called the Wondrously Awakened One. Here only one aspect is set forth; for the rest see the special explanations. His bodily marks and light are fully shown in the contemplation of the Buddha. (Lingzhi Commentary)

As for sutra, in Sanskrit it is called sutra, translated as the conforming doctrine. Conforming has two meanings: above, it conforms to the principle of all Buddhas; below, it conforms to the capacities of beings. Sutra again has many meanings. The Buddha-land opens two: to string together, stringing together the teachings spoken; and to hold, holding the beings to be transformed. In this world there are four: constant, unchanging through the three times; dharma, the same standard throughout the ten directions; a path, traversed alike by past and present; and a canon, honored and observed far and near. (Direct Pointer Commentary)

This sutra is named for the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life because it specifically clarifies the primary and circumstantial adornments of the lord of the land of Ultimate Bliss, and the compassionate skillful means, without being confused with the Buddhas of other directions; it seeks to cause beings to turn their minds single-mindedly and quickly escape birth and death. Contemplation has many gates, adapted to the sharp and dull capacities of beings. Gathered up in the one Buddha, nothing is left uncovered. The nine grades are spread apart and ten thousand streams all converge; without departing from the reward and transformation bodies one suddenly penetrates the dharmakaya, and without leaving the shared land one directly ascends to the stage of successor. Such skillful means are without match or peer. Those who encounter this sutra should arouse a determined mind, firm in their vow, and within this very body hasten to be born in that land. (Concise Treatise)

I reflect that Sakyamuni in this world sends us forth and Amitabha from that land comes to welcome; that land calls and this world sends, how could one not go? One should only diligently apply himself to the Dharma, taking the end of life as the limit, and abandoning this body of reward, immediately realize the eternal bliss of that dharma-nature! (Four-Fascicle Commentary)
Translated by the Western Regions Tripitaka Master Kalayasas of the Liu Song dynasty

The Liu Song is so called to distinguish it from the Zhao Song. Liu Yu received the abdication of the Jin, named his state Song, and set the capital at Jiankang (present-day Jiangning in Jiangsu). It held the provinces of today's Yangtze and Pearl River basins. In all, eight sovereigns and fifty-nine years. (From year 1492 before the common era (420) to year 1433 before the common era (479).) The throne passed to the Southern Qi. (Annotated Commentary)
The name Western Regions points to the kingdoms west of Dunhuang. In ancient times it was commonly used to refer to the kingdoms of India. (Annotated Commentary)

Tripitaka means the sutras, the discipline, and the treatises. A Master of Dharma is so called because he takes the Dharma of the Tripitaka as his teacher; also, because he is deeply versed in it and teaches and transforms beings.

Kalayasas is the name of the chief translator. The Biographies of Monks say: Kalayasas means well-praised in his time; he was a man of the Western Regions, by nature upright and with few desires, thoroughly versed in the Tripitaka and especially skilled in the meditation of dhyana. In the early Yuanjia era of the Song he reached the capital. Emperor Wen deeply admired him and commanded him to reside at the Daolin Hermitage on Mount Zhongshan. The monk Seng Han requested him to translate this sutra, with the Sutra of the Medicine King and the Contemplation. Han was the amanuensis. Later he traveled in Shu and returned to die at Jiangling at the age of sixty. To translate is to turn the Sanskrit text into the Chinese text.
The major divisions are three: 1. the Preface Section, 2. the Main Teaching Section, and 3. the Circulation Section.
A. First, the Preface Section has two parts
1. The confidence-verifying preface
2. The initiating preface
B. First, the confidence-verifying preface

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Rajagrha, on Mount Grdhrakuta, together with a great assembly of monks, twelve hundred and fifty in all, and thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, with the prince of the Dharma Manjusri at their head.
The verification of faith has six points:

First, Thus refers to the Dharma spoken in the main teaching section. Conforming to principle is called thus and being free of what is not is called true. It can be decisively trusted, hence it says thus.

Second, have I heard means that Ananda personally heard it from the Buddha, showing it is not his own words. All dharmas are selfless; being selfless, there is no hearer. Yet following the worldly convention of provisional designation, it is spoken of as I.

Third, at one time means from the gathering of the assembly to the end of the session. That single period of time distinguishes it from other times. When the Tathagata speaks scriptures the times are immeasurable and cannot be fixed, so it says at one time. Moreover, the years, months, days, and hours of the western region and this land differ, and when circulated elsewhere people find them hard to understand. Furthermore, in some scriptures a single sermon could not be completed, and it was only later at the council that the text was assembled, so the before and after are not uniform and hard to mark. That is, in this present sutra, King Ajatasatru committed evil, the Tathagata spoke the sutra, and Ananda repeated it; how could these be the same time? Therefore a single phrase encompasses all.

Fourth, Buddha is the lord who proclaims the teaching, showing it is no other person. It points to the Sakyamuni master who revealed the Pure Land. Buddha is translated as awakening. Awakening oneself differs from ordinary beings; awakening others differs from the two vehicles; and the fullness of awakening differs from the bodhisattvas, hence it is called the Great Awakened One.
Fifth, in the city of Rajagrha below is the place where the sutra was spoken. (The above are recorded from the Lingzhi Commentary.)

Rajagrha: in Sanskrit it is called Rajagrha, in the kingdom of Magadha in central India. King Bimbisara moved his capital here from the old city of the Upper Reed Palace. The city is surrounded by five mountains, and Grdhrakuta is one of them. The Tiantai Commentary gives three reasons for the mountain's name: first, from the rule of the kings; second, from removing the fear of fire; third, from the place of those afraid of wrongdoing. The text is too long to record here. For detail see the Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom, chapter three, and the Records of the Western Regions, chapter nine.

Grdhrakuta is translated as Vulture Peak, where the sages and spiritual sages dwell. It is also called Vulture Head, the peak resembling a vulture; or it is where many vultures roost, and so it is named. The Tiantai Commentary gives three explanations: from the sage-spirits dwelling there; from the peak's shape resembling a vulture; and from the roosting of vultures. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Sixth, the great monks and others are the assembly of identical hearing. There are two groups: the assembly of sravakas and the assembly of bodhisattvas. If we speak of their vows, the bodhisattvas come first; here taking their deportment, the sravakas are placed first. (Lingzhi Commentary)
First is said of the assembly of sravakas

Together means in common. In Sanskrit it is called mahas, translated as great. Great has three meanings: great, many, and supreme. Revered by heavenly kings and great beings, it is called great because its merit is great. Comprehensively understanding both inner and outer scriptures, it is called many because its knowledge is vast. Rising above the ninety-five kinds of teachers, it is called supreme because its views are supreme. (Tiantai Commentary, first

A monk, by his provisional name, has three meanings: seeker of alms, one who terrifies Mara, and one who destroys evil. In the fruit stage the arhat also has three: one worthy of offerings, one who destroys the thieves (of defilements), and one beyond birth. In Sanskrit, samgha is translated as assembly. With four or more persons, harmonious and without dispute, performing the karmic rites and recitation of precepts, able to accomplish all matters of destroying evil and producing good, it is therefore called an assembly. (Lingzhi Commentary)

The twelve hundred and fifty are his retinue disciples. The three Kashyapas together had a thousand disciples, and Maudgalyayana and Sariputra together two hundred and fifty. Formerly they were all fire-worshipping heretics who long endured bitter toil without realizing anything; but once they saw the Tathagata they immediately ascended to the fruit of sainthood. Grateful for the Buddha's deep kindness, they always attended him. (Lingzhi Commentary)
Being together at one place is called accompanying.
Next is said of the assembly of bodhisattvas

A bodhisattva, fully stated as bodhisattva, is translated as an enlightened being, one who enlightens all beings in an expansive way. Thirty-two thousand is the number. (The Lingzhi Commentary says: The thirty-two thousand are the leaders and their retinue.) Manjusri is translated as Wondrous Virtue, also called Wondrous Head, and again Wondrous Auspiciousness. Entering the proper position of the Dharma, he is called prince of the Dharma. His wisdom and virtue alone stand supreme, so he is the leader. (Direct Pointer Commentary)

The Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says: The Buddha is the king of the Dharma, and the bodhisattvas, entering the proper position of the Dharma through the ten grounds, are all called princes of the Dharma. The bodhisattvas, as those raised in the home of the Buddha, king of the Dharma, are all princes of the Dharma. Yet in the scriptures Manjusri is widely called prince of the Dharma, because he sits above the two attendants of the World-honored One and is the foremost Dharma-son aiding the Buddha's teaching. The Annotations on the Lotus Sutra, Words and Sentences: The scriptures call Manjusri prince of the Dharma for two reasons: first, among the princes, virtue is deferred to Manjusri; second, in the various scriptures Manjusri is the head of the bodhisattva assembly. The head of the assembly is the leader, the principal seat of the whole assembly. (Annotated Commentary)
The above lists the great and lesser assemblies to establish confidence. All scriptures commonly have this and it is also called the common preface. (Direct Pointer Commentary)

The larger and smaller Amitabha Sutras list the assemblies very broadly, while this sutra is the most concise. The translations suited their times and each had its own intention. It should also list the assemblies of humans, gods, and the miscellaneous beings, for below in the circulation section it says: the immeasurable gods, dragons, yakshas, and so on. From this we know that in the preface too this is abbreviated. (Lingzhi Commentary)
B. Second, the initiating preface
1. First, the imprisonment of the king is made clear
2. Second, the intent to harm the mother is shown

The circumstances of the various scriptures differ according to their events. This present sutra takes killing and treason as its initiating cause for roughly two intentions: first, to reveal that the beings of this world are utterly detestable, for one would dare to harm even his own parent, let alone others; the intention is to cause beings of the latter age to delight in the Pure Land. Second, to show that the capacity of this world does not think of liberation and rebirth in that land unless it meets extreme suffering, so below Vaidehi says: Speak widely to me of a place without sorrow and distress; I shall be born there and take no delight in the defiled evil world of Jambudvipa. (Lingzhi Commentary)
C. First, the imprisonment of the king has four parts
1. Prince Ajatasatru imprisons the king his father
2. The queen consort secretly offers the porridge and ghee
3. The king requests the precepts to sustain his mind
4. Sustained by both the Dharma and food he does not die
D. First, Prince Ajatasatru imprisons the king his father

At that time, in the great city of Rajagrha, there was a prince named Ajatasatru. Following the instruction of the evil friend Devadatta, he seized the king his father Bimbisara and shut him in an inner chamber of seven walls, commanding all the ministers that none might go to him.
At that time shows that the Buddha was then at the capital preaching, distinguishing the occasion from times when he travelled to teach in other kingdoms. (Direct Pointer Commentary)

Ajatasatru is translated as the unborn enemy, because even in the womb he had conceived hatred and harm toward his father. Or it is called Balala..., translated as one with a broken finger, because at birth the king ordered him dashed to the ground, but he did not die and a finger was broken. (Direct Pointer Commentary)
Following means believing another's teaching and obeying another's intent; this is called following. (Annotated Commentary)

Devadatta, fully stated as Devadatta, is translated as heaven-heated; when he was born the hearts of all the gods were agitated with heat, knowing that when he appeared in the world he must surely destroy the Triple Gem. (Also named Heaven-given.) He was the son of King Dronodana, cousin of the Buddha and elder brother of Ananda. He had thirty marks. On renouncing the world he recited six myriad dharma-collections and the twelve Vedas. When he saw the Tathagata revered by kings and ministers and that offerings abounded, envy arose in his heart, and he went to the Buddha to ask to lead the assembly. The Buddha reproved him, and so he plotted to harm the Buddha. Ananda, not knowing, taught him the method of supernatural power. He entered the mountains and cultivated it, attaining the five supernormal knowledges. Then he thought: who shall be my benefactor? Prince Ajatasatru has the marks of a great king. So he manifested various transformations to delude him into belief and said to the prince: I shall become a new Buddha and you a new king; is this not a delight! Thereupon he pushed a rock down to crush the Buddha. The secret guardian Vajrapani threatened him with his vajra, and the broken rock flew out and injured the Buddha's toe, drawing the Tathagata's blood. He called himself a Buddha and taught beings with five dharmas, and the five hundred new learners such as Susima were converted by his evil teaching, forming a separate assembly to beg alms and a separate observance, which split the wheel of the Dharma-sangha. The nun Utpalavarna met him on the road and reproved him, and he struck her and put out her eye, thus killing an arhat. He committed the three heinous offenses and was born in hell. Ajatasatru killed his father and harmed his mother, together the five heinous offenses. All these are great and powerful deeds of transformation by the great ones; whether adverse or compliant, none is without benefit to beings, and all are for the sake of preventing living beings of later ages from committing heinous acts. The sutra says: He reveals that he has the three poisons and again manifests the appearance of wrong views. My disciples are like this, as skillful means to save sentient beings. The Nirvana Sutra also says that Devadatta did not in truth fall into hell or commit evil, and so on. Truly this is not a state within the scope of sravakas or pratyekabuddhas; it is only the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Suddenly seizing the king's person is called apprehending; having got him, not releasing him is called imprisoning. Speaking of the father specifically indicates the utmost closeness of kin; king shows his rank; Bimbisara shows his name. As for being shut in an inner chamber of seven walls, what was done was grave and the matter not trifling; it could not be a light confinement among men without any guarding at all. But since the king's palace naturally excludes outsiders, only the ministers and officials, long accustomed to attending him, could, unless strictly forbidden, find occasion for secret communication. Therefore he caused the inner and outer to have no contact and shut him within seven walls. (Four-Fascicle Commentary)

Bimbisara is translated as solid and real, and also named Stable Shadow; in both cases the name arises from the solidity of his bodily form. Some translate it as handsome in countenance. The seven-walled chamber was not a matter of going and coming; adding further restraints, he intended to starve him to death. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Such events are all the skillful devices of the great beings manifesting transformation, walking in what is not the Way yet penetrating the Buddha Way. The roots of beings differ, so their entry into the Way differs; one against and one for, both spread the Way and benefit beings. They manifest the practice of the uninterrupted hell without anger or affliction. Ajatasatru manifested the adverse in order to stop evil people of later times from committing treason. (Tiantai Commentary)

Ajatasatru had enmity before birth, the cause of the imprisonment; following the evil teaching is the condition; the seven-walled chamber with the ban on entry is the method; the seizing and confining is the deed. The sutra takes the imprisonment of the father as its initiating cause for two reasons: first, Bimbisara, formerly while hunting deer on Mount Vipula and finding nothing, saw a sage and conceived an angry mind of hatred, drove him away, and had him killed. The sage, at death, vowed to be born as his son and to harm him with heart and mouth. If the grudge were not repaid, one could not prevent people from innocent harm. The Surangama Sutra says that the retributions of hatred harm through the thought of parents, like the owl and the mirror-beetle and such classes; this is precisely that meaning. Second, if the son had not committed treason, he would have been greedy for wealth and honor and could never have been led to hear the Dharma and attain the fruit, being wearied of the suffering of this Saha world. (Direct Pointer Commentary)
D. Second, the queen consort secretly offers the porridge and ghee

The queen consort, named Vaidehi, revering the king, bathed and purified herself, mixed ghee and honey with porridge and smeared it on her body, and within her necklaces and girdles concealed a vessel of grape juice, and secretly brought it to the king.
Vaidehi was the consort of King Bimbisara and the mother of Ajatasatru. (Annotated Commentary)

Vaidehi is translated as reflection. Having received this name first, it became a portent of today's request for contemplation. She bathed to purify her body, smeared it with porridge and ghee, and the hollowed ornaments could hold fruit juice. She slipped into the deep chamber, hence it is called secretly. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Ghee is pronounced su, belongs to the class of curds, and is made from the milk of cows and goats. Bran is parched flour; wheat is steamed and ground into powder to make the bran. (Annotated Commentary)

I privately think: Of deep affection, none surpasses husband and wife. The king was imprisoned within seven walls and the ministers were forbidden to go to him; how could the lady's heart not be moved to tears? Knowing clearly he would starve to death, how could her heart bear it? Offering ghee and porridge to the king is only natural. (Commentary Elucidation)
D. Third, the king requests the precepts to sustain his mind, in three parts
1. The king requests Maudgalyayana
2. Maudgalyayana responds to the occasion
3. The Buddha sends Purnamaitrayani-putra to preach
E. First, the king requests Maudgalyayana

At that time the great king, having eaten the porridge and drunk the juice, asked for water to rinse his mouth. When he had rinsed, he pressed his palms together in reverence, and facing Mount Grdhrakuta bowed from afar to the World-honored One and said: Great Maudgalyayana is my kinsman and friend; may he rouse his compassion and confer upon me the eight precepts!

Maudgalyayana is translated as the Maudgalya clan. In antiquity a sage gathered and ate beans, and from this the clan was named. He was the king's family teacher, therefore called kinsman and friend. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Saying that the great Maudgalyayana was kinsman and friend has two meanings: while in lay life Maudgalyayana was the king's close relative; having gone forth, he became his family teacher. Going and coming within the palace, there was no obstruction at all. But being a relative in lay life and called a friend in renunciation, hence he is called kinsman and friend. (Four-Fascicle Commentary)

The eight precepts are the eight precepts of the one-day observance. The Sutra of the Ten Good Karmic Precepts says: The eight precepts' observance is what the Buddhas and Tathagatas of the past and present established for lay people as the dharma of renunciation. First, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to engage in sexual conduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to drink wine; sixth, not to sit on a high and broad bed; seventh, not to engage in song, dance, and music, nor to go to watch and listen, nor to wear perfume or adornments; eighth, not to eat beyond the midday meal. (Annotated Commentary)
E. Second, Maudgalyayana responds to the occasion
At that time Maudgalyayana, flying like a hawk or falcon, swiftly reached the king's place; he did so daily and conferred the eight precepts on the king.

Maudgalyayana, having known this, responded to the occasion and went. Like a hawk or falcon in flight was the simile for the swiftness of his supernormal powers. Falcon, pronounced xun; the dictionary says it is a bird of prey, a fierce bird. The eight precepts' observance is limited to one day and one night, so it was received anew each day. (Lingzhi Commentary)
The hawk is a bird of prey; the falcon is the smallest of the hawk class. (Annotated Commentary)
E. Third, the Buddha sends Purnamaitrayani-putra to preach
The World-honored One also sent the Venerable Purna to preach the Dharma to the king.

Purna is translated as son of Full Compassion, named from his parents. Among preachers of the Dharma he is the foremost, skilled at opening and guiding, so he was especially sent. (Lingzhi Commentary)
D. Fourth, sustained by both the Dharma and food he does not die
Thus for a period of twenty-one days the king ate the porridge and ghee and, because he heard the Dharma, his countenance became serene and joyful.

The king, by eating and hearing the Dharma, did not die over many days. This precisely clarifies that the queen long offered food to remove hunger and thirst, and the two sages again inwardly sustained him with the precepts, skilfully opening the king's mind. Food can prolong life and the precepts nourish the spirit; losing the suffering and banishing sorrow, they caused his countenance to be serene and joyful. (Four-Fascicle Commentary)
C. Second, the intent to harm the mother is shown
1. The unfilial son harms his mother
2. The compassionate mother seeks help
D. First, the unfilial son harms his mother, in three parts
1. First, he is about to harm his mother
2. Second, he is stopped by the ministers' remonstrance
3. Third, he orders her shut away
E. First, he is about to harm his mother
At that time Ajatasatru asked the gatekeeper: Does the king my father still live?

At that time the gatekeeper reported: Great king, the queen consort smears her body with ghee and honey, and hides juice in her necklaces to bring to the king; and the monks Maudgalyayana and Purna come through the air and preach the Dharma to the king, so that none can forbid it.

At that time Ajatasatru, hearing this, was angry with his mother and said: My mother is a thief! She is the companion of thieves! And those evil monks, with their deluding spells, cause this wicked king not to die for so many days! Then he seized a sharp sword and would have killed his mother.

First, the king asked whether he was still alive. Then in the passage beginning at that time the gatekeeper, they report to him with the facts. Then in the passage beginning at that time Ajatasatru, the king, having heard, was angry. I privately think: First, if a man lives beyond seven days there must be a reason: either the water of concentration sustains his spirit, or the power of the Way adds support. Had the king truly died, the gatekeeper would certainly have come to report. Now twenty-one days had passed with no tidings of death, so Ajatasatru asked: Does he still live? The words still and the question mark are the pivot of the question. Second, the gatekeeper answered with facts and said none could forbid it for two reasons: first, the queen is the mistress, so how would any dare to forbid her; second, the two sages arrived through the air, so how could they be stopped. With these two considerations he said it could not be done. Third, what Ajatasatru originally wanted was only for the king to be gone so he could face south as sovereign; hearing that he still lived, how could he not be angry? The anger within issuing from the mouth, he suddenly forgot the kindness of foster care and cursed: My mother is a thief! Thief means a robber, one who robs me of the immediate fulfillment of my sovereign wish. Those monks are also thieves, coming daily to the palace to be my mother's companions, hence she is the companion of thieves! He knew well the monks were not evil men; he wanted his father dead, and they, with their power of incantation, kept him alive, putting obstacles in my way, so he calls them evil men. He knew well the incantation's power was great; calling it deluding is also a curse. Because his rising anger could not be checked, he seized the sword to harm his mother. The commentary resolves the difficulty: He should have killed the gatekeeper, yet he wanted to harm his mother because the gatekeeper had his answer; the king had first commanded the ministers be forbidden without speaking of women, and the monks flew in through the air, which I could not prevent. Though the king coveted the kingdom and killed his father, he still did not violate the Dharma. (Elucidation)
E. Second, he is stopped by the ministers' remonstrance

At that time there was a minister named Candraprabha, intelligent and wise; together with Jivaka, they made obeisance to the king and said: Great king, we have heard it said in the Veda treatises that from the beginning of the kalpa there have been wicked kings who, coveting the kingdom, killed their fathers, eighteen thousand of them. But never have we heard of one who, without justification, killed his mother. Now, for this act of killing and treason, the king would defile the Kshatriya caste, and we cannot bear to hear of it. You are a Candala! We should no longer remain here! Then the two ministers, having spoken these words, pressed their hands upon their swords and withdrew, walking backwards.
